newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban defy quit-ultimatum and bomb foes.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban defy quit-ultimatum and bomb foes.

text.p: Fighting flared north of Kabul on Wednesday as radical Islamic Taleban leaders defied an ultimatum to quit the city and neighbouring Iran called for a peaceful settlement by all factions.
Taleban also opened sudden peace talks with powerful northern warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum at a meeting apparently brokered by Pakistan, another influential neighbour.
The worsening conflict in Afghanistan has aroused concern in both countries and elsewhere in Central Asia. Some fear that Taleban's Islamic zeal could spill over their borders.
Taleban warplanes bombed the strategic town of Jabal os-Siraj, held by ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, for a second successive day, witnesses said.
The Taleban movement hit back with air raids as it rejected his demand to abandon Kabul, seized by Islamic fighters on September 27.

Afghan sources said Taleban's acting foreign minister Mullah Mohammad Ghaus met Dostum for peace talks, along with Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar and Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction leader Karim Khalili.

The four-hour meeting at Qala-i-Jangi fort outside Mazar-i-Sharif decided to resume talks on Thursday on the proposed formation of a commission to decide about the country's political future, a spokesman for Dostum said.
The meeting was the first known high-level contact between Dostum and the Taleban, whose militia has ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government from Kabul.
Babar's visit was his second to Mazar-i-Sharif in two days.
Neighbouring Pakistan, denying charges that it supports the Taleban, offered to set up peace talks between the Afghan warring sides after Dostum aligned himself with Rabbani against the Taleban.

In Geneva, the International Committee of the Red Cross said at least 800 people have been wounded in recent fighting in Afghanistan and hospitals are full of victims from the frontline north of Kabul.
Acting information minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told Reuters the Taleban was strong enough to defend the city and dismissed a withdraw-or-else ultimatum by former defence minister Masood.
The British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) quoted Masood as demanding on Tuesday the purist Islamic movement withdraw from the city or face bloodshed and destruction.
"This type of ultimatum does not have any significance. If it had, then we would have then we would not have set up our movement," Mutaqi said.

Masood has swept out of his Panjsher valley stronghold some 80 km (60 miles) north of Kabul, rolling Taleban forces back across the plain north of the capital in the past week and taking the towns of Jabal os-Siraj and Charikar.

But the Taleban hit back on Wednesday, bombing Jabal os- Siraj for a second day and pushing the frontline a few km (miles) further north from where it was on Tuesday, Reuters reporter Kurt Schork reported from Jabal os-Siraj.
Jabal os-Siraj sits 90 km (60 miles) north of Kabul astride the main highway linking the capital to northern Afghanistan.

Travellers reported fighting south of Charikar, around the village of Qara Bagh, some 30 km (20 miles) north of Kabul and about 20 km (12 miles) south of Charikar. Most of Qara Bagh was in Taleban hands after briefly falling to Masood forces.
Despite the shifting frontline, Masood's lightning advance towards the capital appears to have largely halted.

Masood's position strengthened on Monday when the northern Uzbek leader Dostum recognised the ousted government of Rabbani, Masood's political mentor, apparently ranging a solid coalition against the Taleban.
But there was no immediate sign of Dostum's forces entering the battle and no sign of any impending assault on the city, which was calm on Wednesday.
Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said in the Kazakh capital Almaty that the crisis in Afghanistan could not be resolved by force and called on all factions to negotiate.
"We believe that (the) Afghanistan problem doesn't have a military solution," Velayati said after discussing the fighting in Afghanistan with Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev.
"All factions should sit down together, talk together to reach a peaceful settlement in Afghanistan," he told reporters.

Shi'ite Moslem Iran, which has evacuated all but one of its embassy staff from Kabul in the past few days, has criticised the Sunni Moslem Taleban, saying its attempts to impose a harsh version of Islamic Sharia law are giving Islam a bad name.
